svg.title: Four ways to distribute labels: LDP, RSVP-TE, BGP and segment routing
svg.desc: Four columns, each answering who assigns the label, what problem it solves and where it fits. LDP assigns labels for each IGP prefix, follows the shortest path and cannot do traffic engineering; it is the default transport. RSVP-TE signals a path and reserves bandwidth, so it can steer traffic and protect it explicitly, at the cost of per-flow state on every router. BGP assigns the VPN label per VRF, and this is what makes L3VPN possible. Segment routing distributes labels as a range inside the IGP itself, needs no per-flow state, and is displacing LDP and RSVP in carrier cores. A bottom band gives the current default recommendation: LDP for transport, BGP for service, and segment routing when a new core is being built.
svg.text: Four label distributors, four different questions answered
Do not ask “which protocol”; ask “what am I trying to place under control”
LDP
Labels per IGP prefix
Follows whatever the IGP chose.
Assign, advertise, swap, done.
Cannot do traffic engineering:
the path is the shortest path.
The default transport. Low state,
no reservations, no surprises.
RSVP-TE
Signals a path and a reservation
CSPF picks the path from the
traffic-engineering database.
State per tunnel on every router
along the path: the scaling limit.
Use when a small number of flows
must be steered and protected.
BGP (MP-BGP)
Labels per VRF, per route
The VPN label travels with the
VPNv4 route as an attribute.
This is the label that identifies
the customer, not the road.
Without it there is no L3VPN,
only a labelled core.
Segment routing
Labels as an IGP index range
Each node gets a label; the
source lists the path as a stack.
No per-flow state in the core,
so TE stops being a scaling problem.
Where new cores are built, this is
replacing LDP and RSVP-TE.
HOW THEY COMBINE IN A REAL NETWORK
Transport layer: LDP (or segment routing) gives every PE a label path to every other PE. It knows nothing about customers and never should.
Service layer: MP-BGP advertises VPNv4 routes, each carrying its own VPN label and its route targets. This is where customer identity lives.
The layering rule that prevents most L3VPN outages: never let the transport layer depend on the service layer, and never let a service
decision leak into transport. LDP following the IGP is a feature: it means one failure is repaired once, by the IGP, not twice by two protocols
with different timers. When someone proposes redistributing VPN routes into the underlay “to make it simpler”, that is the failure being designed in.
Lab check: break the IGP adjacency between two P routers and confirm the LSP reroutes without any BGP session changing state.
